1.title: The verb falar — present tense -ar
1.intro: One verb gives you nine working forms: three sentence forms (statement, negative, question) across three tenses. First see the whole scheme, then drill it to automatic. This lesson takes the present tense of -ar verbs.
blocks: -ar verbs in the present change their ending by person: eu falo, tu falas, ele/ela/você fala, nós falamos, eles/elas/vocês falam.
The negative is the word «não» before the verb: eu não falo. A question keeps the same word order, just with a rising intonation: tu falas?

This lesson has eight -ar verbs, and they all conjugate the same way: falar (to speak), morar (to live), trabalhar (to work), estudar (to study), comprar (to buy), tomar (to have/drink), almoçar (to have lunch), pagar (to pay).
European norm: «tu» (you) is widely used in everyday speech. Questions are often built with «é que»: «Onde é que tu moras?» — «Where do you live?».
You can drop the pronoun — the verb ending already shows the person: «Falo português» = «Eu falo português». Both versions count as correct in the exercises.

2.title: Pronouns and question words
2.topic: eu, tu, ele… + onde, quando, quem, o que, como, porquê
2.intro: Seven personal pronouns and six question words open almost any conversation. In European Portuguese a question is most often built with the connector «é que».
blocks: Pronouns: eu (I), tu (you), ele/ela (he/she), você (you, polite), nós (we), eles/elas (they), vocês (you, plural).
Question words: onde (where), quando (when), quem (who), o que (what), como (how), porque/porquê (why). Question pattern: «Onde é que tu moras?» — literally «Where is it that you live?».
In Portugal «tu» is the normal way to address friends and peers. «Você» is polite-neutral, and is often dropped entirely: «Mora aqui?» — «Do you live here?».

3.title: Ser and Estar — two verbs for «to be»
3.intro: Portuguese has two verbs for «to be». Ser is for the permanent: who you are, where you're from, your job. Estar is for state and location: how you feel, where you are right now, whether the café is open.
blocks: Ser: eu sou, tu és, ele/ela é, nós somos, eles são. Estar: eu estou, tu estás, ele/ela está, nós estamos, eles estão.
Compare: «O café é ótimo» — the café is great in general (a property). «O café está fechado» — the café is closed right now (a state).
When introducing themselves, the Portuguese put an article before the name: «Eu sou o Alex», «Ela é a Ana». That's the norm, not a mistake.

4.title: -er verbs — present tense
4.intro: The second group of verbs ends in -er. The logic is the same as -ar; only the vowel in the endings changes: como, comes, come, comemos, comem.
blocks: Comer (to eat): eu como, tu comes, ele come, nós comemos, eles comem. The same pattern: beber (to drink), viver (to live), aprender (to learn), vender (to sell).
Perceber is the main Portuguese verb for «to understand» (compreender is the bookish synonym). «Não percebo» is survival phrase number one.
A sandwich in European Portuguese is «uma sandes» (in Brazil — sanduíche). The landlord of a rented flat is «o senhorio».

5.title: -ir verbs — present tense
5.intro: The third and last group is -ir verbs. The endings are almost like -er; only the «we» form differs: abrimos.
blocks: Abrir (to open): eu abro, tu abres, ele abre, nós abrimos, eles abrem. Also: partir (to leave), decidir (to decide).
Two useful verbs slightly change their stem in the «I» form: dormir → durmo (I sleep), preferir → prefiro (I prefer). The other forms are regular: dormes, prefere…
«A que horas abre…?» — «What time does … open?» — the standard question about shops, museums and pharmacies.

6.title: Past tense — Pretérito Perfeito
6.intro: Pretérito Perfeito is the main past tense: completed actions. «Yesterday I worked, ate, went to bed» — all of that is PPS.
blocks: -ar endings: falei, falaste, falou, falámos, falaram. -er endings: comi, comeste, comeu, comemos, comeram. -ir endings: parti, partiste, partiu, partimos, partiram.
A European detail: in the «we» form the -ar past is written with an accent — «jantámos» (we had dinner), while the present has none — «jantamos» (we have dinner).
The most useful irregular form: fui — «I was» and «I went» (ser and ir share the past): «Fui ao supermercado» — «I went to the supermarket».

7.title: Future tense — ir + infinitive
7.intro: The future in spoken Portuguese is the verb ir (to go) + infinitive: «vou falar» — «I'm going to speak». Just like English «going to».
blocks: Ir: eu vou, tu vais, ele vai, nós vamos, eles vão. Then any infinitive: vou comprar (I'll buy), vais gostar (you'll like it), vamos jantar (we'll have dinner).
The present can also serve as a future when there's a time marker: «Amanhã trabalho» — «Tomorrow I work».
«Vamos beber um café?» is the standard Portuguese invitation. To agree: «Vamos!»

There is also a second, more formal way — the synthetic future: falarei (I will speak), comerei (I will eat), partirei (I will leave). In speech, ir + infinitive is more common, but the synthetic future appears in texts and formal speech. The «Verb forms» trainer drills both.

8.title: Estar a + infinitive — action right now
8.topic: Estou a trabalhar — I'm working (right now)
8.intro: An action happening right now is expressed in Portugal with estar a + infinitive: «Estou a trabalhar» — «I'm working (at this moment)».
blocks: Estar is conjugated (estou, estás, está, estamos, estão), the infinitive stays the same: estou a falar, estás a comer, estamos a chegar.
This is the hallmark of European Portuguese. In Brazil they say «estou falando» — in Portugal always «estou a falar».
«Não estou a perceber» — «I don't understand (what's happening/being said) right now» — one of the most common phrases.

9.title: Modal verbs — want, can, must
9.topic: poder, querer, ter de, dever, precisar de
9.intro: Five key verbs: querer (to want), poder (to be able), ter de (to have to), dever (should), precisar de (to need). A plain infinitive follows them.
blocks: Querer: quero, queres, quer, queremos, querem. Poder: posso, podes, pode, podemos, podem. Ter: tenho, tens, tem, temos, têm (+ de: tenho de ir — I have to go).
«Posso…?» is the all-purpose polite question: Posso pagar com cartão? Posso experimentar? Posso deixar a mala aqui?
In a café you order with querer: «Quero um galão, por favor» (a galão is coffee with milk in a tall glass). Or softer: «Queria…» — «I'd like…».

10.title: Articles and contractions — no, na, do, ao, pelo
10.topic: Prepositions of place + em/de/a/por with articles; ficar and há
10.intro: Articles: o, a, os, as. The prepositions em, de, a, por merge with them into short words — giving the ever-present no, na, do, da, ao, à, pelo, pela.
blocks: em + o = no (in), em + a = na; de + o = do (from/of), de + a = da; a + o = ao (to), a + a = à; por + o = pelo (through/along), por + a = pela.
Ficar — «to be located» for buildings and places: «A farmácia fica ao lado do café» — «The pharmacy is next to the café». Há — «there is»: «Há uma farmácia aqui perto?»
Multibanco is the Portuguese cash machine (and a whole payment system). Os correios — the post office. A paragem — the bus stop.

11.title: Possessives — my, your, our + the verb ter
11.topic: o meu, a tua, o nosso; tenho, tens, tem
11.intro: «My house» in Portuguese is «a minha casa», with an article before the possessive. Gender and number agree with the thing, not the owner.
blocks: o meu / a minha / os meus / as minhas (my); o teu / a tua (your); o nosso / a nossa (our); o vosso / a vossa (your, plural). Ter (to have): tenho, tens, tem, temos, têm.
«O seu» usually means «your» (polite). For «his/her» the Portuguese say dele/dela: «o carro dele» — his car.
«Tens horas?» — «Have you got the time?» (literally «do you have hours?»). A renda — the rent. O troco — the change.

12.title: Movement and transport
12.topic: ir de metro, apanhar o autocarro, vir de, até
12.intro: How to get there: ir de + transport (de metro, de carro, de autocarro) or a pé (on foot). «To catch / take» is the verb apanhar.
blocks: Apanhar: apanho o autocarro (I catch the bus), apanhamos um táxi (we take a taxi). Vir (to come): venho, vens, vem, vimos, vêm.
Para — direction «for good / all the way» (vou para casa — I'm going home), a — «briefly» (vou ao banco — to the bank and back). Até — «as far as»: até à estação.
O elétrico — the Lisbon tram. O comboio — the train (in Brazil trem). Connosco — «with us» (the European form).

13.title: Adjectives and demonstratives
13.intro: An adjective agrees with the noun in gender and number: vinho tinto, casa bonita, praias lindas. Demonstratives: este (this, near me), esse (that, near you), aquele (that one, far away).
blocks: Gostar de — «to like»: gosto de café, gostas de bacalhau? With demonstratives, de merges: gosto deste restaurante (de + este).
Comparison: mais caro (do) que — more expensive than; melhor — better; o melhor — the best.
Giro/gira — colloquial «cool, nice» (Portugal only). Sossegado — calm, quiet (about a neighbourhood, a café).

14.title: Numbers, time and prices
14.topic: What time it is, how much it costs, days of the week
14.intro: Numbers, hours and prices — what you need every day: at the café, the market, the station. Plus the days of the week and the question «Que horas são?».
blocks: 1–12: um, dois, três, quatro, cinco, seis, sete, oito, nove, dez, onze, doze. Tens: vinte, trinta, quarenta, cinquenta… cem (100).
Time: É uma hora (one o'clock), São duas/três horas. At what time — às: às oito e meia (at 8:30). Price: custa — it costs, custam — they cost.
Days: segunda, terça, quarta, quinta, sexta (weekdays — «-feira»), sábado, domingo. «À segunda» — on Mondays. Many museums are closed à segunda!

15.title: Pretérito Imperfeito — used to, would
15.topic: Habits and background in the past: morava, era, tinha
15.intro: The second past tense — for habits, background and descriptions: «I used to live in Porto», «coffee was cheaper». Not a finished event (that's PPS) but a picture of the past.
blocks: -ar endings: morava, moravas, morava, morávamos, moravam. -er/-ir endings: bebia, bebias, bebia, bebíamos, bebiam.
Four key irregulars: era (was), tinha (had), ia (used to go), havia (there was).
Compare: «Morei no Porto dois anos» — a fact, a finished period (PPS). «Morava no Porto quando era estudante» — background, a habitual state (Imperfeito).

16.title: Everyday phrases — politeness and survival
16.topic: Set phrases for every day: café, street, conversation
16.intro: The final lesson — ready-made phrases the Portuguese say every day. Learn them whole, like words: they glue together everything you already know.
blocks: Dizer (to say/tell): digo, dizes, diz, dizemos, dizem. «Como se diz…?» — «How do you say…?» — your learning tool forever.
Obrigado is said by a man, obrigada by a woman. The reply: «De nada» or «Não tem de quê».
Pois é — «yeah, true». Se calhar — «maybe». Está bem — «okay, fine». Combinado — «it's settled». These little words make speech come alive.
